newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Accused Colombian drug king detained in Venezuela.
newsitem.headline: Accused Colombian drug king detained in Venezuela.

text.p: A reputed Colombian drug lord described as one of the wealthiest and most sought-after men in his country was arrested on Friday in neighboring Venezuela, authorities said.

Justo Pastor Perafan, 50, whose personal fortune has been estimated at $12 billion by Colombia's leading news magazine Semana was detained during the night in this capital city of Tachira state, just across the border from Colombia.

Perafan, whose extensive business interests extend to Madrid, Rome, Moscow and South Africa, had been actively sought for more than a year in Colombia, where police posted a $500,000 reward for information leading to his arrest.

Tachira Governor Ricardo Mendez Moreno said Perafan, who had been living in San Cristobal for the past year or so, would be taken by military plane later in the day to the Venezuelan capital Caracas, pending his possible extradition.
Colombian police and security chiefs flew to San Cristobal before dawn to seek his immediate extradition.
Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia thanked Venezuela for Perafan's arrest and said Bogota would discuss with Caracas how best to send him back to Colombia.

But she did not rule out that Venezuela may choose to extradite him to the United States instead. "He has a criminal record in that country too," she said on Colombian radio, confirming that Perafan is wanted on drug charges in New York.
He is also sought in Costa Rica and Panama where he was once arrested in 1982 but managed to slip out of the country without facing charges.

Gen. Gerardo Briceno, a commander of Venezuela's National Guard in San Cristobal, said Perafan did not resist arrest when police detained him at around 1 a.m. (0500 GMT) at a small commercial center, capping months of intelligence work.

He told reporters the former army sergeant and head of the Bogota drug cartel was using false papers that identified him as Rafael Antonio Cruz. He had changed his appearance through plastic surgery but was identified through his fingerprints.
Colombian Justice Minister Carlos Medellin said in Bogota that Perafan's arrest "marked the end of one the most complex chapters in drug trafficking."

With the arrest of the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers and most other leaders of the Cali drug mob in 1995 and 1996, Perafan was allegedly the top Colombian drug lord still at large. Wanted posters featuring his picture and the $500,000 reward have been flashed nightly on Colombian television for most of last year.
Perafan, speaking to reporters in his cell, emphatically denied he had anything to do with drugs and said he was "unjustly persecuted in Colombia for political reasons."
"I am not a drug trafficker, never been one and never will be one. I'm just an honest businessman," he said.
Colombian National Police chief Rosso Jose Serrano, who flew to San Cristobal before dawn and personally helped identify Perafan, noted that all drug traffickers claimed their innocence.
"We're very happy, just as happy as if we had captured him ourselves, because we have him behind bars," he said.
Perafan has been accused of shipping more than 4,400 pounds (2,000 kg) of cocaine to Italy and other countries.

The alleged drug baron had ties to Colombian politicians. Defense minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez stepped down last month when it was revealed that Perafan had donated $3,000 to his congressional election campaign in 1989.

Semana magazine last year said Perafan's illicit business empire included partial ownership of a mine in South Africa and an oil pipeline in the former Soviet Union. Many of his properties in Colombia, including a luxury hotel in Tolima province and most of Baru island, a resort near the Caribbean port city of Cartagena, have been confiscated by police.
"Perafan's fortune is one of the biggest there is," Gen. Luis Enrique Montenegro, Colombia's secret police chief, told Semana. "It could even surpass that of the Rodriguez Orejuela brothers."
